practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is an example of an abiotic component of an ecosystem?
A) Decomposer fungi
B) Soil moisture
C) Earthworms
D) Algae
practice_questions.marks: B) Soil moisture [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two biomes found at high latitudes.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Polar / tundra
• Boreal / coniferous forest
• Temperate forest (in higher mid-latitudes)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two ways in which abiotic and biotic components of an ecosystem are interdependent.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Soil supplies plants with water and nutrients (1) which support animals further up the food chain (2 — developed).
• Decomposer bacteria and fungi break down dead matter (1) returning nutrients to the soil for new plant growth (2 — developed).
• Climate (rainfall, temperature) determines vegetation type (1) which in turn determines the animal communities present (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain why tropical rainforests cluster around the equator.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies equator latitude (0-10°N/S). Explains the global atmospheric circulation: rising warm air at the Equator (Hadley cell) cools and produces heavy convectional rainfall almost daily. Combination of constant warmth (25-28°C) and 2000+ mm rainfall sustains rainforest. Names major locations (Amazon, Congo Basin, South East Asia).
Secure: Identifies climate plus location with one cause.
Developing: Names rainforest locations without explaining climate cause.
Emerging: Generic; no causes.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the global circulation of the atmosphere produces the pattern of biomes from the equator to the tropics.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explains rising air at the equator producing tropical rainforests; descending air at 20-30°N/S producing hot deserts; rising air at temperate latitudes producing forests; descending polar air producing tundra. Uses named biomes (Sahara at 20-30°N, Amazon at the Equator). Connects atmosphere to climate to vegetation to animal communities. Acknowledges the role of ocean currents in modifying coastal climates.
Secure: Two zones explained with named biomes.
Developing: One zone explained.
Emerging: Names biomes without atmospheric mechanism.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“Climate is the most important factor determining the location of the world's biomes.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss the role of climate
• discuss other factors (ocean currents, soil, altitude, human activity)
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Climate — latitude controls temperature and rainfall, producing predictable biome belts (Amazon equatorial rainforest, Sahara at 20-30°N). Other factors — ocean currents shift coastal climates (the Gulf Stream gives the UK temperate forest at 50°N when continental Russia at the same latitude is taiga); altitude creates vertical biome zones (rainforest to alpine tundra in the Andes); human activity has cleared 47% of original forest globally for farmland. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether climate is dominant or merely the framework that other factors modify.
Secure: Both sides with named examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; no examples; no clear judgement.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.content_html:
What Is an Ecosystem?

An ecosystem is a community of living things and the physical conditions they share. Every ecosystem on the planet is built from the same two types of components. Abiotic components are the non-living parts: weather, climate, soil, rock and water. Biotic components are the living parts: plants, animals, fungi, bacteria and humans.

The two are interdependent — remove one and the others change. Cut down a rainforest tree and the soil around it dries faster, the water cycle slows, animals lose their habitat and bacteria in the leaf litter starve. Reduce sea-surface temperature by even one degree and coral algae begin to bleach, fish populations migrate, and entire reef ecosystems collapse. Understanding interdependence is the foundation of every ecosystem case study.

Key Fact

Every ecosystem has abiotic components (weather, climate, soil, rock, water) and biotic components (plants, animals, fungi, bacteria, humans). They are interdependent — a change in one affects all the others.

The Global Pattern of Ecosystems

The world's major ecosystems — the biomes — show a clear pattern from the equator to the poles. Polar regions sit at the highest latitudes (above the Arctic and Antarctic Circles), with extreme cold, low precipitation and minimal vegetation. Coral reefs form in shallow tropical seas where water is warm (23-29°C), clear and salty. Hot deserts like the Sahara, Atacama and Australian Outback occupy 20-30° latitude north and south, where descending air from the global atmospheric circulation produces dry conditions. Grasslands form in mid-latitudes (the Argentine Pampas, North American Prairies) where rainfall is too low to support forest but high enough for grasses.

Temperate forests dominate mid-latitudes with seasonal climates — UK woodlands, the eastern United States, parts of China and Japan. Tropical rainforests sit in a belt around the equator (Amazon, Congo Basin, South East Asia) where temperatures stay 25-28°C year-round and rainfall exceeds 2000mm. The pattern is not random — it follows the global circulation of the atmosphere, ocean currents and latitude-driven temperature.

At the equator, the sun is high overhead all year, warming air and ocean intensely. Warm air rises, cools and produces heavy convectional rainfall almost daily. The combination of constant warmth and heavy rainfall creates conditions for the most diverse ecosystems on Earth. The Amazon alone is home to an estimated 10% of all known species. Move 10° either way and the rainfall pattern becomes seasonal — rainforest gives way to seasonal forest and savannah.

Climate, Plants and Animals in Each Biome

Each biome has a distinctive climate, plant community and animal community:

  • Polar regions — very cold (-50 to 5°C), little precipitation, slow-growing lichens and mosses, polar bears, seals, penguins (Antarctica only).
  • Coral reefs — warm tropical seas, sunlit shallows; coral colonies form the structure that shelters thousands of fish species, sharks, turtles and molluscs.
  • Tropical rainforests — warm, wet all year; multi-storey vegetation (emergents, canopy, under-storey, ground layer); jaguars, sloths, parrots, vast insect populations.
  • Hot deserts — very hot days, cold nights; cacti, drought-resistant scrub; camels, scorpions, snakes, desert foxes.
  • Temperate forests — four seasons; deciduous oak, beech and ash; deer, foxes, badgers, woodland birds.
  • Grasslands — seasonal rainfall, fertile soils; grasses dominate; herds of bison, antelope, kangaroos.

Vegetation type follows climate. Where temperatures stay warm and rainfall is plentiful, dense forests grow with multiple layers. Where rainfall is seasonal, grasslands or savannahs dominate. Where it is consistently dry, deserts form with sparse, drought-tolerant vegetation. Where it is consistently cold, tundra mosses and lichens are the main plant life. The mapping of climate to vegetation is one of the most predictable relationships in geography.

Key Fact

The six global biomes — polar, coral reef, tropical rainforest, hot desert, grassland, temperate forest — form a predictable pattern from the equator to the poles, controlled by latitude, atmospheric circulation and ocean currents. Climate sets the framework; plants and animals adapt to fit.

Putting It Together

Ecosystems are not random — they sit in a global pattern shaped by latitude, atmosphere and ocean. The interdependence of abiotic and biotic components means a change in one part triggers changes everywhere else. The next two lessons explore two of the most threatened biomes — tropical rainforests and coral reefs — in case-study detail.

before.exam_tip_html: For 4-mark and 6-mark questions on ecosystems, name your biomes and use specific climate data (temperature, rainfall) to explain the global pattern. For 12-mark evaluations of biome management, weigh threats and responses with named examples (Amazon deforestation rate, Great Barrier Reef bleaching events). Avoid generic comments about ‘the environment’ — specificity gets the marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the world's largest tropical rainforest?
A) Madagascan
B) Congo Basin
C) Amazon
D) Australasian
practice_questions.marks: C) Amazon [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two threats to the Amazon rainforest.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Deforestation for cattle ranching
• Deforestation for soya farming
• Illegal logging
• Gold mining
• Climate-change driven drought and forest fires
• Road building
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the rainforest nutrient cycle.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Most nutrients are stored in the biomass (1) rather than in the soil, which is thin and acidic (2 — developed).
• Decomposition is rapid (1) because warm wet conditions accelerate fungi, bacteria and termite activity (2 — developed).
• Released nutrients are taken up immediately by tree roots (1) before they can wash away in heavy rainfall (2 — developed).
• If trees are cleared, the nutrient store is lost (1) and the soil cannot support farming for long (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how the Amazon rainforest is valuable to humans.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies multiple values with statistics. Local — supports 30 million people including 350+ indigenous groups; supplies timber, rubber, Brazil nuts, acai. Regional — stabilises rainfall across South America. Global — stores 100 billion tonnes of carbon, provides 6% of the world's oxygen, source of medicines (quinine, curare). Connects each value to the rainforest process that delivers it.
Secure: Three values with at least one statistic.
Developing: Two values with limited specifics.
Emerging: Generic comments about ‘biodiversity’.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how sustainable management strategies aim to protect the Amazon.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies multiple strategies with specific examples. Indigenous land rights — managed indigenous land has lower deforestation than government-protected zones. Selective logging takes few trees per hectare, leaving canopy intact. Ecotourism — Mamiraua Sustainable Reserve in Brazil generates revenue without clearance. International payments — REDD+ pays countries to keep forests standing. Tightened Brazilian enforcement from 2023 has cut deforestation sharply. Acknowledges trade-offs (development vs protection) and the tipping point at 20-25%.
Secure: Three strategies with named examples.
Developing: Two strategies; effects partial.
Emerging: Generic; few facts.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The international community is doing enough to protect the world's tropical rainforests.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss successful international actions
• discuss limitations and continuing threats
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Successes — REDD+ payments, EU Deforestation Regulation, slowing of Brazilian deforestation since 2023, indigenous land protection, certification schemes (FSC). Limitations — 17% of Amazon already cleared, tipping point at 20-25% looming, illegal logging continues, climate change accelerates drought and fire, demand for soya and beef in rich countries drives clearance. Conclusion explicitly weighs progress against scale of threat. Specific Amazon and global statistics throughout.
Secure: Both sides considered with named examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on rainforests, name your case study (Amazon), give a statistic (17% deforested, 100 billion tonnes carbon stored) and link a process (water cycle, nutrient cycle) to a threat. For 12-mark evaluations, weigh the success of management strategies (indigenous land rights vs ecotourism vs REDD+) before reaching a justified conclusion.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the world's largest coral reef?
A) Florida Reef
B) Andros Coral Reef
C) Great Barrier Reef
D) Red Sea Coral Reef
practice_questions.marks: C) Great Barrier Reef [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two conditions a coral reef needs to grow.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• Warm water (23-29°C)
• Salty water
• Plenty of sunlight
• Clear, low-nutrient water
• Shallow depth (less than 50 m)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two effects of mass bleaching on the Great Barrier Reef.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• Coral polyps expel zooxanthellae algae (1) and turn white as their colour is lost (2 — developed).
• Coral starvation if conditions don't recover (1) leading to large-scale coral death (2 — developed).
• Loss of habitat for thousands of fish, mollusc and turtle species (1) cascading through the food web (2 — developed).
• Tourism revenue affected (1) with parts of the reef closed to visitors after the 2024 event (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how the symbiotic relationship between coral and algae underpins reef ecosystems.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies symbiosis as a close mutually beneficial relationship. Explains both directions: zooxanthellae algae photosynthesise and share sugars and oxygen with coral; coral provides shelter and access to sunlight. Connects this to the productivity that supports 25% of marine species. Acknowledges that disrupting the relationship (through warming, pollution) causes the whole reef to collapse.
Secure: Symbiosis defined with both partners' contributions; some reef ecosystem context.
Developing: One side of the relationship explained.
Emerging: Names symbiosis without mechanism.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activity threatens the Great Barrier Reef.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Identifies multiple human-driven threats with statistics. Climate change — sea-surface temperatures 1-2°C above normal trigger mass bleaching; five events between 2016 and 2024, 75% of the reef affected in 2024. Water pollution — sediment from sugar cane farming, fertiliser run-off feeding crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks. Coastal development — ports and dredging damage reef edges. Connects local pressures to the dominant global driver of climate change.
Secure: Three threats with named examples.
Developing: Two threats with partial explanation.
Emerging: Generic; no statistics.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The Great Barrier Reef can be saved through local management strategies.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss what local management can achieve
• discuss the role of global climate action
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Local management — Marine Protected Areas (344,000 km<sup>2</sup>; 33% no-take), water quality improvements, crown-of-thorns culls, coral gardening, Reef 2050 Plan funding. Climate action — even with perfect local management, scientists project 70-90% reef loss above 1.5°C warming. Global emissions cuts are essential. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether local management buys time without solving the underlying problem.
Secure: Both sides considered with named examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.content_html:
What Is a Coral Reef?

A coral reef is one of the planet's most productive ecosystems. It is built by millions of tiny coral polyps that secrete a hard calcium carbonate skeleton. Inside each polyp lives a microscopic algae called zooxanthellae, which photosynthesises and shares its sugars with the coral in exchange for shelter. This symbiotic relationship is the foundation of every coral reef.

Reefs cover less than 1% of the ocean floor but support an estimated 25% of all marine species — from clownfish and parrotfish to sharks, turtles and giant clams. They form in shallow tropical seas where conditions are perfect: water temperatures between 23 and 29°C, salty water, plenty of sunlight, and clear, low-nutrient conditions that favour coral over algae.

Where Coral Reefs Are

The world's major warm-water coral reefs cluster between 30°N and 30°S. The largest is the Great Barrier Reef off the coast of Queensland, Australia — 2,300 km long, covering 344,000 km2, the world's largest living structure and visible from space. Other significant reefs include the Mesoamerican Barrier Reef from Mexico to Honduras, the Red Sea Reef between Africa and Arabia, the New Caledonia Barrier Reef in the Pacific, the Florida Reef, and the Andros Coral Reef in the Bahamas. Each shares the same conditions but supports a slightly different community of species.

Key Fact

Coral reefs need warm water (23-29°C), salinity, sunlight and clear, low-nutrient conditions. The Great Barrier Reef in Australia is the world's largest, covering 344,000 km2 and supporting 1,500 fish species and 400 coral species.

Reef Nutrient Cycle

Reef ecosystems run on a tight, fast nutrient cycle. Coral polyps catch tiny plankton from the water column at night. Their zooxanthellae photosynthesise during the day, providing sugars and oxygen. When fish or invertebrates die, decomposer bacteria release nutrients quickly back into the water column where they are absorbed by other organisms. Because the surrounding tropical seas are nutrient-poor, almost all the nutrients in a reef stay locked inside the ecosystem — a closed loop that only works because the reef itself is alive and intact.

Case Study: The Great Barrier Reef

The Great Barrier Reef is Australia's most famous natural feature. Its biodiversity is staggering: 1,500 fish species, 400 coral species, 4,000 mollusc species, 240 bird species, plus dugongs, dolphins and humpback whales. Value to humans: the reef supports 64,000 jobs and generates AU$6.4 billion a year in tourism revenue. It protects the Queensland coast from storm waves and provides nurseries for commercial fisheries.

Threats: the Great Barrier Reef has experienced five mass bleaching events between 2016 and 2024 — the most severe in 2024, affecting around 75% of the reef. Bleaching is caused by sea-surface temperatures 1-2°C above normal, often during El Nino years. If the heat doesn't ease, bleached coral dies. Other threats include water pollution from agricultural run-off (sediment from sugar cane farming), crown-of-thorns starfish outbreaks fed by nutrient pollution, and damage from coastal development.

When water becomes too warm, coral polyps expel the zooxanthellae living inside them. The coral turns white — bleached — and immediately starts to starve. If temperatures fall again within weeks, polyps can take new algae back in and recover. If the heat persists, the coral dies. Globally, the planet has lost about half its shallow-water reef cover since 1950, with the rate accelerating as ocean heatwaves become more frequent. Bleaching is the most visible signal of climate change in marine ecosystems.

Australia's Reef 2050 Plan combines several strategies. Marine Protected Areas cover the entire Great Barrier Reef Marine Park (344,000 km2), with no-take zones in 33% of it. Water quality improvements aim to cut sediment and fertiliser run-off from sugar cane farms. Crown-of-thorns starfish culls reduce coral predation. Coral gardening — growing heat-tolerant corals in nurseries and replanting on damaged reefs — is being scaled up. International climate action is the most important: without limiting warming below 1.5°C, scientists project the loss of 70-90% of the reef by 2050.

Key Fact

The Great Barrier Reef has had five mass bleaching events between 2016 and 2024, with up to 75% of the reef affected in 2024. Climate action below 1.5°C is the only strategy that can save the reef long-term, alongside Marine Protected Areas and water quality improvements.

Putting It Together

Coral reefs concentrate enormous biodiversity into shallow tropical seas, supported by the symbiotic relationship between coral polyps and zooxanthellae algae. The Great Barrier Reef shows how climate change, water pollution and coastal development combine to threaten reefs worldwide. Strong exam answers always cite specific reef statistics and connect bleaching to its global cause — ocean warming.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a Low-Income Developing Country (LIDC)?
A) United States
B) China
C) Mozambique
D) Brazil
practice_questions.marks: C) Mozambique [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two indicators used to measure development.
practice_questions.marks:
Award 1 mark each, max 2:
• GNI per capita
• Human Development Index (HDI)
• Internet users per 100 people
• Life expectancy
• Literacy rate / years of schooling
• Infant mortality rate
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe two advantages of using the Human Development Index over GNI per capita.
practice_questions.marks:
Award up to 2 marks per developed point, max 4:
• HDI combines income, life expectancy and schooling (1) giving a more rounded picture of development than money alone (2 — developed).
• HDI captures social progress (1) so a country with high income but low life expectancy or poor schooling scores lower (2 — developed).
• HDI is internationally comparable (1) and updated regularly by the UN (2 — developed).
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe and explain how Advanced Countries (ACs), Emerging and Developing Countries (EDCs) and Low-Income Developing Countries (LIDCs) differ.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Defines all three categories with named examples. ACs — high incomes, high HDI, mature service economies (USA, Japan, UK). EDCs — rising incomes, expanding manufacturing, fast-growing cities (China, India, Brazil). LIDCs — low incomes, agriculture-based, weak infrastructure (Ethiopia, Mozambique, Bangladesh). Uses statistics (HDI scores, GNI figures) to support each.
Secure: Three categories with named examples and clear distinctions.
Developing: Two categories explained.
Emerging: Lists categories without distinction.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain why no single development indicator gives a complete picture of a country's development.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Multiple indicators discussed with limitations. GNI per capita — ignores inequality, informal economies and quality of life. HDI — updates slowly, weights its three components equally. Internet usage — misses older and rural populations. Life expectancy — influenced by healthcare access but not a perfect proxy for wealth. Uses examples (Switzerland HDI 0.962 vs Niger 0.394) to show how multiple indicators give a fuller picture than any single one.
Secure: Three indicators evaluated with limitations.
Developing: Two indicators with partial limitations.
Emerging: Lists indicators without evaluation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
“The traditional ‘developed/developing’ binary is no longer useful for understanding the world.”
Evaluate this statement.
In your answer you should:
• discuss why the binary is criticised
• discuss the AC, EDC and LIDC alternative
• reach a justified conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Balanced argument. Critique — the binary collapses very different countries into one category (China alongside Mozambique); ignores rapid change since 1990; politically loaded. AC/EDC/LIDC alternative — recognises rising EDCs (China 18% of global GDP, India fifth-largest economy); separates them from LIDCs concentrated in sub-Saharan Africa; tracks change over time. Acknowledges that any classification is imperfect — even AC/EDC/LIDC has fuzzy borders and political risks. Conclusion explicitly weighs whether the new categories solve more problems than they create.
Secure: Both sides considered with named examples; conclusion follows the argument.
Developing: One-sided argument; conclusion present but weak.
Emerging: Generic; few facts; no clear judgement.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.content_html:
A Divided World

If you visited Switzerland and Mozambique on consecutive weeks, you would experience two different planets. Average life expectancy is 84 years in one and 60 in the other; school enrolment is 99% versus 70%; GDP per person is over 100,000 USD versus 600. Yet both are members of the United Nations. Development is the technical name for these gaps — and explaining them is one of geography's central tasks.

Development is not just about money. It has three dimensions. Economic development measures wealth and jobs. Social development measures health, education and quality of life. Environmental development measures whether growth is sustainable for future generations. Sustainable development brings the three together — the goal accepted by the UN in 2015 through the 17 Sustainable Development Goals.

Measuring Development

Different indicators reveal different aspects of development. The trick is to use several together rather than relying on any one statistic. Recent decades have seen indicators evolve as understanding of development has deepened.

  • GNI per capita — gross national income divided by population, measured in USD. Simple and globally comparable, but ignores inequality and informal economies.
  • Human Development Index (HDI) — combines life expectancy, years of schooling and GNI per capita into one score from 0 to 1. Recognises that development is more than money. Norway and Switzerland top the HDI; Niger and Chad sit at the bottom.
  • Internet users per 100 people — a 21st-century indicator that captures connectivity and digital infrastructure.

Each indicator has advantages and limits. GNI per capita is comparable but blind to inequality (a country with average income of 20,000 USD could be very equal or very unequal). HDI is more rounded but slow to update. Internet usage misses older or rural populations. Strong development analysis uses multiple indicators rather than relying on one.

Key Fact

GNI per capita measures average wealth but ignores inequality. HDI combines life expectancy, schooling and income but updates slowly. Internet users per 100 captures connectivity but misses older and rural populations. Use multiple indicators for an accurate picture.

Country Categories

The World Bank and UN now use a three-way classification rather than the old ‘developed/developing’ binary:

  • Advanced Countries (ACs) — high incomes, high HDI, mature service economies. Examples: USA, UK, Japan, Germany.
  • Emerging and Developing Countries (EDCs) — rising incomes, expanding manufacturing, fast-growing cities. Examples: China, India, Brazil, Mexico, Indonesia.
  • Low-Income Developing Countries (LIDCs) — low incomes, agriculture-based economies, weak infrastructure, often heavily dependent on aid. Examples: Ethiopia, Mozambique, Bangladesh, Cambodia.

In 1990, China and India were both classified as low-income. By 2024, both had moved into the EDC group. China now produces about 18% of global GDP. India has overtaken China as the world's most populous country and has the world's fifth-largest economy. The development map looks dramatically different from the one in geography textbooks of just 20 years ago. The big challenge today is sub-Saharan Africa, where most LIDCs are concentrated.

Consequences of Uneven Development

Uneven development matters because it shapes almost everything else in a country. People in LIDCs face higher infant mortality, lower educational attainment and shorter lives — an average baby born in Niger has a one-in-twelve chance of dying before its fifth birthday. International migration flows largely from low-development to high-development regions, putting strain on receiving countries and depriving sending countries of skilled workers. Unequal countries struggle to attract investment; without investment, they struggle to develop. The cycle is hard to break, which is why aid, trade and education policies matter so much in international politics. Climate change deepens these gaps further: LIDCs contribute least to global emissions but suffer the worst from droughts, floods and food-supply shocks — an injustice highlighted at every UN climate summit since the 2015 Paris Agreement. Understanding development gaps is therefore not just an academic exercise; it sits at the heart of the world's biggest political and economic decisions.

Switzerland's HDI is 0.962, the world's highest. Niger sits at 0.394, the lowest. Switzerland's life expectancy is 84 years; Niger's is 62. GNI per capita: 88,000 USD in Switzerland; 580 in Niger. The same metrics applied to a single country (Brazil's HDI of 0.760, GNI per capita of 7,500 USD) show that EDCs sit clearly in the middle — ahead of LIDCs but a long way from ACs.

Key Fact

Three categories: Advanced Countries (USA, Japan, UK), Emerging and Developing Countries (China, India, Brazil), and Low-Income Developing Countries (Ethiopia, Mozambique, Bangladesh). The pattern has shifted dramatically since 1990 as China and India joined the EDC group.

Putting It Together

Development is more than wealth: it covers economic, social and environmental progress. Indicators like GNI, HDI and internet usage capture different aspects, and the AC-EDC-LIDC classification reveals patterns that the old binary missed. The next two lessons explore why this uneven world exists and what can be done about it.
before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark questions on development indicators, name two indicators and explain one advantage and one disadvantage of each. For 12-mark evaluations, use specific countries and statistics (Switzerland HDI 0.962, Niger 0.394) to compare ACs, EDCs and LIDCs. Avoid the ‘developed/developing’ binary — OCR examiners specifically reward AC/EDC/LIDC vocabulary.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes bilateral aid?
A) Aid given through international organisations like the World Bank
B) Aid given directly from one government to another
C) Aid donated by charities such as Oxfam
D) Aid sent in the immediate aftermath of a disaster
practice_questions.marks: B) Aid given directly from one government to another [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two types of aid that an LIDC might receive.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct type, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Bilateral aid (government-to-government)
• Multilateral aid (through bodies like the World Bank or UN)
• Emergency / short-term aid
• Long-term development aid
• NGO / charity aid
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how patterns of global trade can hold back development in LIDCs.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description with two distinct trade patterns linked precisely to held-back development. May include LIDCs exporting low-value primary commodities while importing higher-value manufactured goods, and the impact of unstable world prices.
Secure: Clear description of one or two trade patterns with relevant examples (e.g. coffee, cocoa, copper) linked to development.
Developing: Some description of trade and development with limited link between the two.
Emerging: Simple statement that trade is unfair, with no clear link to development.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how colonialism has contributed to uneven development in the world today.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking colonial actions (resource extraction, arbitrary borders, slave trade, lack of investment in local industry) to present-day patterns such as low GNI per capita, weak manufacturing or political instability in former colonies. Specific named examples (e.g. British, French or Belgian colonies in Africa).
Secure: Clear explanation linking two or more colonial impacts to current development with at least one example.
Developing: Some link between colonialism and modern development; explanation may be limited or only one factor used.
Emerging: Simple statement that colonialism caused inequality with no developed reasoning.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain why having valuable natural resources does not always lead to development.
Use one example to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation of the resource curse with named country example (e.g. Democratic Republic of Congo and cobalt, or oil-rich states with low HDI). Links resources to weak governance, profit flowing to elites or transnational corporations, conflict over mining areas, and limited reinvestment.
Secure: Clear explanation of two or more reasons (governance, conflict, unequal profit distribution) with a relevant example.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one reason or one example, with some uncertainty about how resources fail to drive development.
Emerging: Simple point that resources do not always help, with no clear reasoning or example.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Aid does more harm than good for low-income developing countries.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion weighing arguments on both sides with specific evidence. Arguments in support: tied aid forces purchases from donor countries, large loans create debt burdens, free imports can undercut local farmers, corruption can divert funds, long-term aid dependency slows local industry. Arguments against: vaccines and emergency relief save lives (Gavi 17m+ deaths prevented), schools and clinics built (UK aid in Sierra Leone), small-scale NGO projects empower communities, multilateral aid funds infrastructure. Reaches a justified conclusion taking aid type and use into account.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with at least one named example on each side and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion of advantages and disadvantages but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided discussion with little evidence and no clear conclusion.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.content_html:
Why Has Development Been Uneven?

Countries have not all developed at the same rate. Some advanced countries (ACs) such as the UK, Germany and Japan grew rich during industrialisation. Others, including many in sub-Saharan Africa, remain low-income developing countries (LIDCs). The reasons stretch back hundreds of years and continue to shape today’s world. The key causes are colonialism, unfair patterns of trade, dependence on a few natural resources, and the way aid is given.

Key Fact

The four main causes of uneven development are colonialism, trade patterns, natural resources and aid. Each links to the others — colonialism shaped trade routes, which shaped which countries control resources today.

Colonialism and Its Long Shadow

From the 1500s onwards, European powers including Britain, France, Spain, Portugal and Belgium took political control of large parts of Africa, Asia, the Caribbean and the Americas. By 1914 around a quarter of the world’s land area was under British rule alone. Colonisers extracted resources — gold, silver, sugar, cotton, rubber, palm oil — and shipped them back to Europe. Roads, railways and ports were built mainly to move raw materials to coastal export points, not to connect colonies internally.

When colonies gained independence in the 20th century, many were left without diverse industries, well-funded schools or trained professionals. Borders were often drawn by Europeans without regard for local groups, leading to later conflicts. The transatlantic slave trade also removed an estimated 12 million people from West Africa between 1500 and 1870, weakening communities for generations.

Trade Patterns That Lock In Inequality

Trade can grow an economy — or trap it. ACs typically export manufactured goods and services, which earn high prices. LIDCs often export raw primary commodities like cocoa, coffee or copper, whose prices swing wildly on world markets. A poor harvest or a price crash can wipe out government income.

Tariffs and subsidies can make this worse. Wealthy countries sometimes place tariffs on processed imports (such as roasted coffee) but not on raw beans, discouraging LIDCs from adding value at home. The World Trade Organization tries to make rules fairer, but ACs still hold more bargaining power.

A coffee farmer in Ethiopia might earn around 5–10p for the beans in a £3 high-street latte. Most of the value is added later by roasters, transporters and cafes — almost all in ACs. Fair trade schemes try to guarantee a minimum price and a community premium for farmers, but they cover only a small share of the global crop.

Natural Resources: Blessing or Curse?

A country’s natural resources can be a huge advantage. Norway used North Sea oil revenues to build a sovereign wealth fund worth over £1 trillion. But many resource-rich LIDCs experience the resource curse. Profits flow to a small elite, transnational corporations or corrupt officials, leaving ordinary people poor.

Resource wealth can also fuel conflict. The Democratic Republic of Congo holds around 70% of the world’s cobalt — vital for smartphone and electric-car batteries — yet remains one of the poorest countries on Earth, with armed groups fighting for mining areas.

Key Fact

Having valuable resources does not guarantee development. Without good governance, fair contracts and reinvestment of profits, resource wealth can deepen inequality and even cause conflict — this is the resource curse.

Aid: Helpful or Harmful?

Aid means help given from one country or organisation to another. There are several main types:

  • Bilateral aid — given directly from one government to another, often with conditions attached.
  • Multilateral aid — donated through international bodies like the World Bank or UNICEF.
  • Emergency (short-term) aid — sent quickly after disasters such as earthquakes or floods.
  • Long-term development aid — funds schools, clinics, water supplies and training over many years.
  • NGO aid — from charities like Oxfam or WaterAid, often grassroots and small-scale.

Well-targeted aid can save lives and build long-term capacity. The Gavi vaccine alliance is estimated to have prevented over 17 million deaths since 2000. UK aid has built thousands of schools in Sierra Leone, raising literacy rates. Small-scale NGO projects, like installing handpumps or solar panels, often have lasting community benefits because they involve local people in planning.

When Aid Hinders Development

Aid is not always positive. Tied aid forces the receiver to spend the money on goods or contractors from the donor country, so much of the value flows back to the donor. Large loans can leave LIDCs with debts they struggle to repay — some African countries spend more on debt interest than on healthcare. Free imported food can undercut local farmers, and corruption can divert aid before it reaches its target. Critics argue long-term reliance on aid creates a culture of aid dependency, slowing the growth of local industries.
before.exam_tip_html: For the ‘Outline reasons for uneven development’ questions, use the cause-and-effect chain: factor → how it works → result. Always link colonialism to today’s patterns rather than treating it as just history. For 12-mark evaluate questions on aid, weigh up named projects on both sides — for example Gavi vaccines (positive) versus tied loans (negative) — and reach a justified conclusion. Remember the 3 SPaG marks: write in full sentences with accurate spelling of terms like ‘colonialism’ and ‘multilateral’.

practice_questions.text: Describe the relative importance of trade in Nigeria's economic development.

practice_questions.text:
Explain how international investment has shaped Nigeria's recent economic development.
Use named examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation using two or more named investments and showing both benefits and drawbacks. May include oil TNCs (Shell, ExxonMobil, Chevron) creating jobs and tax revenue but causing environmental damage in the Niger Delta; MTN providing mobile networks; Chinese investment in railways, power stations and Lekki deep-sea port. Recognises that profits can flow overseas.
Secure: Clear explanation of two named investments with at least one benefit and one drawback.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one named example, with some uncertainty about long-term impact.
Emerging: Simple statement about foreign companies in Nigeria, with no specific examples.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Nigeria has reached the take-off stage of Rostow's model of economic development.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence from your case study to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion using specific evidence on both sides and reaching a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: oil, telecoms and fintech sectors growing fast; new infrastructure such as Lekki deep-sea port and railways; urban middle class in Lagos and Abuja; over 200 million mobile connections. Arguments against: rural north remains heavily agricultural and poorer; Boko Haram insurgency holds back development; over-reliance on a single export; high inequality and youth unemployment; Rostow's model itself has been criticised for ignoring colonial history and global inequality.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named evidence and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided argument with little evidence.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.content_html:
Why Nigeria?

Nigeria is a strong country case study because it is the most populous nation in Africa with around 220 million people, the continent’s largest economy, and an emerging and developing country (EDC). It is changing fast: oil wealth, a young workforce and a booming tech sector pull development forward, while regional inequality, conflict in the north and reliance on a single export hold it back. Studying Nigeria lets us see why development is rarely smooth or even.

Key Fact

Nigeria sits in West Africa on the Gulf of Guinea. Its capital is Abuja, its largest city Lagos has over 15 million people, and its main export is crude oil, which still earns roughly 80% of export revenue.

Location and Environmental Context

Nigeria stretches from the wet, forested south on the coast to the dry Sahel in the north. The Niger and Benue rivers cross the country, supporting farming and fishing. The south has a tropical climate suited to crops like cocoa, oil palm and yam. The north is drier and is more prone to drought and desertification, which damages crops and pushes families to migrate. Oil and natural gas reserves under the Niger Delta and offshore are the country’s most valuable resources.

Politics and International Relationships

Nigeria gained independence from Britain in 1960. After decades of military rule, democratic government returned in 1999. Nigeria is a member of the Commonwealth, the African Union and OPEC (the oil-exporting countries’ group). It works with the UK, USA and increasingly China on trade and investment. Internal conflicts — especially the Boko Haram insurgency in the north — have damaged farming areas and pushed millions of people from their homes.

Trade: Imports and Exports

Crude oil and natural gas dominate exports, with India, Spain, the Netherlands and the USA as key buyers. Cocoa, sesame seeds and rubber are smaller exports. Imports are very different — Nigeria buys in machinery, vehicles, refined petroleum (because it has too few working refineries), wheat and medicines, mostly from China, India and Europe. This pattern, exporting low-value primary goods and importing high-value manufactures, is typical of many EDCs.

Because oil supplies most government income, world price changes shake the whole economy. When oil prices fell in 2014 and again during the 2020 pandemic, Nigeria’s currency (the naira) weakened and the country slipped into recession. Diversifying into farming, manufacturing and tech is now a major government goal.

International Investment

Foreign companies, called transnational corporations (TNCs), play a huge role in Nigeria. Shell, ExxonMobil and Chevron extract oil. South Africa’s MTN runs the largest mobile phone network. Chinese firms have funded railways, power stations and the new Lekki deep-sea port. Investment brings jobs, infrastructure and tax income, but profits often flow back overseas, and oil spills in the Niger Delta have damaged farming and fishing communities.

Population and Employment

Nigeria has a very young population — the median age is around 18, compared with 40 in the UK. Around half of workers are in farming, especially in the north. The service sector has grown quickly, including banking, retail and the ‘Nollywood’ film industry, which produces over 2,000 films a year. Manufacturing is still small. The informal sector employs millions, providing income but little protection.

Key Fact

Nigeria’s median age is roughly 18, with around 60% of people under 25. This gives a huge potential workforce, but the country must create millions of new jobs and school places each year to match the growth.

Social Factors: Education, Health and Technology

Education access has improved — primary school enrolment is now over 60% — but quality varies sharply between cities and rural areas, and over 10 million children are still out of school. Healthcare is mixed: life expectancy is around 55 years, well below the UK’s 81. Mobile phone use has leapt forward, with more than 200 million phone connections, and platforms like mobile banking apps have brought finance to people who never had a bank account. The Lagos tech hub, sometimes called ‘Yabacon Valley’, has produced fintech firms valued at over a billion dollars.

An Aid Project: Polio Eradication

Nigeria was the last African country with wild polio, but a partnership between the World Health Organization, UNICEF, the Bill & Melinda Gates Foundation and Rotary International funded vaccination teams that reached almost every village. In 2020 Africa was declared free of wild polio. The project shows how multilateral aid, when combined with local volunteers and clear targets, can deliver life-changing results.

Rostow’s model sets out five stages: traditional society, preconditions for take-off, take-off, drive to maturity, and high mass consumption. Most geographers place Nigeria around stage 3, ‘take-off’: a few sectors (oil, telecoms, fintech) are growing fast, infrastructure is improving, and a small middle class has appeared. Critics say the model is too simple — it assumes all countries follow the same path that Western nations did, ignoring colonialism, climate and global inequality.
before.conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Nigeria is an EDC of around 220 million people whose growth is driven by oil, telecoms and a fast-growing tech sector, but held back by regional inequality and over-reliance on oil exports.
  • Trade is unbalanced: high-value oil and gas exports against high-value manufactured imports, with TNCs and Chinese investment shaping the economy.
  • Using Rostow’s model, Nigeria is often placed at the ‘take-off’ stage, although the model has limits because it ignores history and global power.
before.exam_tip_html: Country case study questions reward specific, place-based detail. Aim to use at least three named facts (population around 220 million, oil earns about 80% of export revenue, life expectancy around 55, polio eradicated 2020) rather than vague statements. For 12-mark evaluations on Rostow, weigh up evidence that Nigeria is in ‘take-off’ against limits to that view, then conclude. Watch your spelling on names like Niger, Niger Delta and Nollywood for SPaG marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following defines a megacity?
A) Any capital city
B) A city with over 1 million people
C) A city with over 10 million people
D) A city where most people work in services
practice_questions.marks: C) A city with over 10 million people [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two pull factors that attract people to Lagos.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct pull factor, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Greater chance of paid work / formal jobs
• Better schools and education
• Better healthcare
• Wider entertainment, culture and family connections
• Tech and creative industries (Nollywood, fintech)
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the global pattern of megacities has changed since 1950.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of the change with figures. May include only New York and Tokyo as megacities in 1950, around 10 by 1990 and over 30 today. Notes the shift from ACs to LIDCs and EDCs, and the rise of Asian and African megacities such as Delhi, Shanghai, Dhaka, Lagos and Kinshasa.
Secure: Clear description of the global shift with at least one named example.
Developing: Some description of growth but limited use of figures or examples.
Emerging: Simple statement that more cities have got bigger.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain the social and environmental consequences of rapid urbanisation in an LIDC or EDC city you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking causes of rapid urbanisation in Lagos to clear social and environmental impacts. May include informal settlements like Makoko (around 60% of residents in informal housing), traffic congestion and air pollution from older vehicles, flooding worsened by blocked drains, waste-management pressure at sites such as Olusosun.
Secure: Clear explanation of two consequences (one social, one environmental) with named examples.
Developing: Some explanation but with limited examples or only one type of consequence.
Emerging: Simple list of problems with no clear case study reference.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how migration has shaped the character and ways of life of one major city in an LIDC or EDC.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation using Lagos as case study. Covers internal migration from rural Nigeria (especially the north) and international migration from neighbouring states like Benin, Togo and Ghana. Links migration to multi-ethnic communities (Yoruba, Igbo, Hausa), markets like Balogun and Computer Village, the spread of Afrobeats and Nollywood, and to the divide between high-rise districts like Victoria Island and informal settlements like Makoko.
Secure: Clear explanation of how migration has changed Lagos with at least two named features and one figure.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one named example, with some uncertainty about the link between migration and ways of life.
Emerging: Simple statement that many groups live in Lagos with little supporting detail.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Sustainable strategies have successfully tackled the challenges facing Lagos.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence from your case study.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion weighing strategies on both sides with specific evidence and a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: Bus Rapid Transit lanes move commuters faster than cars; Blue Line metro (opened 2023) cuts journeys from over an hour to about 20 minutes; Lekki deep-sea port spreads economic activity east; Eko Atlantic reclaims flood-resilient land. Arguments against: housing shortages and informal settlements such as Makoko continue; traffic and pollution remain severe; Eko Atlantic is criticised for being for the wealthy; flooding still affects many districts; the gap between rich and poor is widening.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named strategies and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided discussion with little evidence.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is a natural cause of climate change?
A) Burning of coal in power stations
B) Deforestation in the Amazon
C) Variations in the Earth's orbit (Milankovitch cycles)
D) Cattle farming
practice_questions.marks: C) Variations in the Earth's orbit (Milankovitch cycles) [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two sources of evidence used to study past climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct source, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Ice cores
• Tree rings (dendrochronology)
• Global temperature records / instrumental records
• Paintings and diaries
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how ice cores are used as evidence of past climate change.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description of the process. May include drilling deep into ice sheets in Antarctica or Greenland; layers of compacted snow trap air bubbles; analysing those bubbles gives carbon dioxide concentrations; oxygen isotopes give past temperatures; record reaches back over 800,000 years.
Secure: Clear description of two stages of the method with at least one figure or named ice sheet.
Developing: Some description but limited link to climate evidence.
Emerging: Simple statement that scientists drill ice with no clear method.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how human activities have contributed to the enhanced greenhouse effect.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking specific human activities to higher greenhouse-gas concentrations and warming. May include burning fossil fuels in power stations and vehicles releasing carbon dioxide; deforestation reducing carbon absorption; methane from cattle farming and rice paddies; CO2 rising from around 280 ppm in 1850 to over 420 ppm today; link to about 1.1°C global warming.
Secure: Clear explanation of two human activities with figures and link to warming.
Developing: Some explanation of human activities but limited link to the greenhouse effect.
Emerging: Simple statement that humans cause warming with no developed reasoning.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain how natural causes can also contribute to changes in the Earth's climate.
Use named examples in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation of two or more natural causes with named examples. Solar output (Maunder Minimum 1645–1715 linked to Little Ice Age cooling); Milankovitch cycles pacing long ice ages; volcanic activity (Mount Pinatubo 1991 cooling global temperatures by around 0.5°C). Recognises that natural causes operate on different time scales from current human-driven change.
Secure: Clear explanation of two natural causes with at least one named example.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one natural cause, with some uncertainty about its impact.
Emerging: Simple list of natural causes with no examples.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Modern climate change is mostly the result of human activity rather than natural cycles.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion weighing evidence on both sides and reaching a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: CO2 levels rising from 280 ppm to over 420 ppm; rate of change far faster than past natural cycles; ice-core record over 800,000 years shows no comparable spike; warming closely tracks the rise in fossil-fuel use since the Industrial Revolution; about 1.1°C of warming since 1850; Arctic sea-ice loss roughly 40% since the 1980s. Arguments referencing natural variability: orbital cycles, solar output (Maunder Minimum) and volcanic eruptions have caused past changes; some natural variability still occurs alongside human warming. Reaches a justified conclusion that human activity is the dominant driver of recent rapid change.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named evidence and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided argument with little evidence.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark explain questions on climate change causes, set out at least one natural cause and one human cause and link each to a process. Use evidence terms exactly — ice cores, tree rings, paintings and diaries, instrumental records — and pair the evidence with the time scale it covers (ice cores 800,000 years, instrumental records since 1850s). For 12-mark evaluations, weigh natural variability against the unprecedented speed and scale of modern warming, and conclude with a clear judgement.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following is the minimum sea-surface temperature needed for a tropical storm to form?
A) 18°C
B) 22°C
C) 27°C
D) 32°C
practice_questions.marks: C) 27°C [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify the three atmospheric circulation cells found in each hemisphere.
practice_questions.marks:
Two marks for naming all three correctly: Hadley cell, Ferrel cell and Polar cell. Award one mark for two correct.
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe the global distribution of tropical storms.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description with named locations and latitude band. May include concentration around 5–30° north and south of the equator; main areas the Atlantic, West Pacific, Bay of Bengal and around northern Australia; absent from the equator itself and from cooler ocean basins.
Secure: Clear description of distribution with at least one named area and reference to latitude.
Developing: Some description of distribution with limited reference to specific places.
Emerging: Simple statement that storms are tropical with no detail.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how the global atmospheric circulation creates the world's hot deserts.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking the Hadley cell to deserts. May include warm moist air rising at the equator, releasing rain over rainforests, drifting polewards as drier air aloft, sinking at around 30° latitude, warming by compression, suppressing cloud and rainfall. Names major deserts (Sahara, Arabian, Kalahari, Australian Outback, south-west USA).
Secure: Clear explanation of two stages with at least one named desert.
Developing: Some explanation but limited link between the cell and deserts.
Emerging: Simple statement that deserts are dry, with no clear cause.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the conditions and processes that lead to the formation of a tropical storm.
Use named examples or features in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation that names the four conditions (sea-surface temperature ≥27°C; about 70m of warm water; low wind shear; 5–30° from the equator) and links them to processes. Describes warm moist air rising, water vapour condensing and releasing energy, air spiralling inwards under the Coriolis effect, formation of the eye and eyewall.
Secure: Clear explanation of three conditions with at least one process linked correctly.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one or two conditions with weak link to formation.
Emerging: Simple list of conditions with no process explanation.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Climate change is making tropical storms more dangerous.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion separating frequency from intensity, with specific evidence and a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: warmer sea-surface temperatures fuel stronger storms; more Category 4 and 5 storms in recent decades; storms are dumping more rainfall and producing larger storm surges; rising sea levels worsen coastal flooding. Arguments against: total number of named storms each year (around 80–90 globally) has not clearly risen; some basins show year-to-year variability rather than long-term trends; better warning and evacuation save more lives than in the past. Reaches a justified conclusion that storms are becoming more dangerous in intensity and impact, even if not in number.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named evidence and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but evidence may be limited and conclusion may not be fully justified.
Emerging: One-sided argument with little evidence.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.exam_tip_html: For 6-mark explain questions on tropical storm formation, structure your answer around the four conditions (sea temperature, depth of warm water, wind shear, latitude) and link each to a process. For 12-mark evaluations on whether storms are becoming more dangerous, separate the number of storms from their intensity, and use evidence such as warmer ocean temperatures and increased rainfall. Use precise terms — eye, eyewall, Coriolis effect — to pick up SPaG and specialist vocabulary marks.

practice_questions.text:
Which one of the following best describes El Nino?
A) A cool phase of the Pacific Ocean linked to flooding in Australia
B) A warm phase of the Pacific Ocean linked to drought in Australia
C) A storm system in the Indian Ocean
D) A type of monsoon over India
practice_questions.marks: B) A warm phase of the Pacific Ocean linked to drought in Australia [1 mark]

practice_questions.text: Identify two ways that Australians adapted to the Millennium Drought.
practice_questions.marks:
One mark for each correct adaptation, up to two marks. Acceptable answers include:
• Building desalination plants in Sydney, Perth, Melbourne or Adelaide
• Domestic water restrictions / hosepipe bans
• Rainwater tanks and greywater reuse
• Drip irrigation and drought-tolerant crops
• Murray-Darling Basin Plan (2012)
• Improved ENSO forecasting from the Bureau of Meteorology
[2 marks]

practice_questions.text: Describe how the trade winds change during an El Nino event.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Clear description that in normal years strong trade winds blow east-to-west, pushing warm water towards Australia and Indonesia, and that during El Nino these winds weaken or reverse, allowing the warm pool of water to slosh back east, taking rainfall with it.
Secure: Clear description of the change in trade winds with at least one location named.
Developing: Some description but limited link between wind change and rainfall pattern.
Emerging: Simple statement that winds change.
[4 marks]

practice_questions.text: Explain how El Nino events can lead to drought in Australia.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained explanation linking weakened trade winds to warmer water in the central/eastern Pacific, rainfall shifting east towards South America, and dry conditions over Australia. Notes the link to higher fire risk and falling reservoir levels. May include reference to the Millennium Drought 2001–2009 or 2015–16 El Nino as supporting examples.
Secure: Clear explanation of two stages with at least one named example.
Developing: Some explanation but limited link between Pacific changes and Australian rainfall.
Emerging: Simple statement that El Nino causes drought.
[6 marks]

practice_questions.text:
Explain the effects of one drought event on people and the environment.
Use a named case study in your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sophisticated explanation using the Millennium Drought (2001–2009) with named effects on both people and the environment. People: wheat harvests fell 36% in 2002; livestock losses; reservoir levels below 30%; water restrictions; rural mental-health crisis and migration. Environment: Murray-Darling lower reaches failed to reach the sea; wetlands shrank; river red gum die-off; Black Saturday bushfires February 2009 (173 deaths); 2009 Sydney dust storm.
Secure: Clear explanation of two human and one environmental effect with named figures.
Developing: Limited explanation, perhaps one type of effect or weak case study detail.
Emerging: Simple list of impacts with no named figures.
[8 marks]

practice_questions.text:
'Adaptation has successfully reduced the impact of drought in your case study area.'
Discuss this view.
Use evidence from the case study you have studied.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained discussion with named adaptations on both sides and a justified conclusion. Arguments in support: large desalination plants in Sydney, Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide give drought-proof city water; permanent water-saving rules and rainwater tanks have cut household demand; drought-tolerant wheat and drip irrigation reduce farm losses; the Murray-Darling Basin Plan (2012) sets caps on river extractions; better ENSO forecasting allows planning ahead. Arguments against: desalination is energy-hungry and expensive; the Basin Plan has been weakened by political lobbying; many smaller farms still went out of business; recent El Nino events of 2018–19 still caused major stress; long-term climate projections show drying continues. Reaches a justified conclusion that Australia is more resilient but not drought-proof.
Secure: Clear two-sided discussion with named adaptations and a reasoned conclusion.
Developing: Some discussion but limited evidence and unjustified conclusion.
Emerging: One-sided argument with little evidence.
[12 marks plus 3 SPaG]

before.content_html:
What Is Drought?

A drought is a long period of lower-than-average rainfall that causes water shortages. Droughts can last months or many years, and they range from mild dry spells to disasters that destroy harvests and force communities to move. Drought is one of the world’s most damaging natural hazards because it affects food, drinking water, ecosystems and energy — everything that life depends on.

Key Fact

El Nino warms the central and eastern Pacific Ocean and is linked to drought in Australia, Indonesia and parts of southern Africa. La Nina cools that same Pacific region and is linked to drought in the southern USA and parts of South America.

El Nino and La Nina Explained

In a normal year, strong trade winds push warm surface waters across the Pacific from South America towards Indonesia and Australia. Warm, moist air rises in the western Pacific and brings heavy rainfall to Australia and South-East Asia. The cool eastern Pacific, off Peru, has rich fisheries.

During El Nino, the trade winds weaken or even reverse. The warm pool of water sloshes back eastwards. Rain that would normally fall on Australia and Indonesia instead falls over the eastern Pacific or Peru. Droughts follow in the western Pacific. La Nina is the mirror image — trade winds blow harder, the Pacific east of South America cools, and Australia and Indonesia receive heavier rainfall while the south-west USA, Argentina and parts of east Africa can dry out. The full pattern is called the El Nino–Southern Oscillation, or ENSO.

Strong El Nino and La Nina events occur on average every 3 to 7 years, although the cycle is not regular. Major El Nino events in 1997–98, 2015–16 and 2023–24 caused severe droughts and wildfires across the western Pacific, while the major La Nina from 2020 to 2022 brought repeated flooding to eastern Australia.

Case Study: The Millennium Drought, Australia (2001–2009)

Australia is highly exposed to ENSO. Between 2001 and 2009 south-eastern Australia experienced its worst drought since records began — the Millennium Drought. The Murray-Darling Basin, which produces around 40% of Australia’s farm output, lost more than half its inflows. The drought coincided with the strong El Nino of 2002 and a series of weaker El Nino events through the decade, plus higher background temperatures from climate change.

Effects on People

Wheat harvests fell by 36% in 2002 alone, and livestock numbers were cut sharply as farmers sold animals they could not water. Many family-run farms went out of business. City reservoirs around Melbourne, Adelaide and Sydney dropped below 30% capacity. Water restrictions banned hosepipes and limited shower times. Mental-health services reported a sharp rise in stress and depression in farming communities, and the Bureau of Statistics linked the drought to increased rural-to-urban migration.

Effects on the Environment

River flows in the Murray-Darling fell so low that the lower reaches stopped reaching the sea. Wetlands shrank, killing river red gum trees and threatening waterbirds. Bushfires intensified, including the ‘Black Saturday’ fires of February 2009 in Victoria, which killed 173 people. Dust storms swept thousands of kilometres — in September 2009 a single storm dumped red dust across Sydney, lowering visibility to less than 100m.

Key Fact

The Murray-Darling Basin produces around 40% of Australia’s farm output. During the Millennium Drought (2001–2009) it lost more than half of its normal river inflows, and Black Saturday bushfires (February 2009) killed 173 people.

How People Adapted

Australia’s response shows a wide range of adaptation strategies:

  • Water-saving in cities — nationwide rules limited garden watering. Households fitted dual-flush toilets and rainwater tanks; greywater (used water from showers and basins) was reused for gardens.
  • New water sources — large desalination plants opened in Sydney, Perth, Melbourne and Adelaide between 2006 and 2012, removing salt from sea water to give a drought-proof supply.
  • Smarter farming — many farmers shifted to drip irrigation, drought-tolerant wheat varieties, and crops needing less water like canola.
  • Murray-Darling Basin Plan (2012) — this huge agreement caps how much water farmers can take from the rivers, leaving more for the environment and downstream communities.
  • Better forecasting — the Bureau of Meteorology now publishes ENSO outlooks so farmers and water managers can plan ahead.

By the time El Nino returned in 2015–16 and again in 2018–19, Australian cities were able to keep water flowing using their desalination plants and stricter rules. Farming losses, while still significant, were less severe than in 2002. Critics argue desalination is energy-hungry and expensive, and that the Murray-Darling Basin Plan has been weakened by political pressure from large agricultural users. The drought has not gone away — long-term climate projections suggest south-eastern Australia will keep trending drier.
before.exam_tip_html: Drought case-study questions reward precise figures and named places. Aim to use at least three: Murray-Darling produces 40% of Australia’s farm output, Black Saturday killed 173 people, wheat harvests fell 36% in 2002. Distinguish El Nino (warm Pacific, drought in Australia/Indonesia) from La Nina (cool Pacific, drought in the south-west USA and parts of South America). For 12-mark evaluations, weigh how well adaptation worked using two named strategies and reach a justified conclusion.
